title: The blessings, alone
tomorrow: what does a chant for safety actually ask for?

cards: Gratitude lists, vision boards, the friend who signs every post hashtag blessed. Everyone has a working theory of what a blessing is.

In this sutta, a deity comes to Jeta's Grove near Savatthi late at night, so bright the whole grove lights up, and asks the Buddha straight out: many have wondered what the highest blessing is. Tell me.
He answers with a list. And every verse ends the same way: this is the highest blessing. Which raises today's argument.
If they're all the highest, which one comes first?

teach.h: ALMOST NOTHING FALLS FROM THE SKY.
teach.b: Look at what's on the list. Almost nothing falls from the sky. Not keeping company with fools, and keeping company with the wise.
Much learning, and a craft well learned. Supporting your mother and father, caring for your family, work that harms no one. Giving, patience, humility, contentment, gratitude.
And near the end: seeing the noble truths, nibbana, a mind that doesn't shake when the world's winds hit it. Tradition says people in the Buddha's day argued about lucky signs.
This list turns luck into conduct, which is why Buddhists chant it at blessings and new beginnings. Now the two readings.
Some teachers read it as a ladder.

teach.h: THE OTHER: EACH ONE IS COMPLETE.
teach.b: It starts with your friends and climbs on purpose, each step steadying you for the next, up to a mind nothing can shake. On that view, the end of the list really is higher, and that's a comfort: you know where it leads.
Every verse says the highest, and they take it at its word. Supporting a parent isn't a low rung under meditation; done fully, it's complete. The ladder asks: then why this order?
The refrain asks: then why call each one highest? The sutta doesn't settle it. It just keeps saying it.

how: In Theravada communities the Mangala Sutta is chanted by monks at house blessings, weddings and other new beginnings, and lay Buddhists learn its verses as a guide to everyday conduct.

games.q: your study group splits. one side says the list is a ladder, climbing to nibbana; the other says each blessing is the highest. give the ladder side's best case.
o: it climbs on purpose: each blessing steadies you for the next, toward a mind that won't shake
the ladder side thinks family duties don't really count for much
the ladder side just likes ranking things and wants a winner
games.why: the list does move from friends and work toward the noble truths and nibbana. the other side's best answer: the refrain gives every step the same name.

practice: Count your blessings the sutta's way, one finger for each: a wise friend, a skill you've learned, someone who raised you, a time you were patient, something you're grateful for today.
When you run out of fingers, rest your hands and stay with the last one you counted.

wordCard.voice: The blessings: the Buddha's answer to a deity's question, a list of things you do, each verse ending, this is the highest blessing.

orig.note: Pali: blessing, auspicious sign; the word every verse of the sutta turns on.
